synopsis: The booklet recommends importance sampling or accelerated evaluation for rare-event evaluation, particularly small-probability estimation, while identifying the independent evidence base as on-road [f10336, f7261, f7268]. Michigan's 2016 research validated a statistical acceleration method for rare crashes and conflicts, reporting acceleration factors of 300–100,000 for car-following and 2,000–20,000 for lane changes; related 2017 published work showed very large lane-change evaluation speed-ups [f1779, f1781, f1782, f6847]. These methods deliberately oversample dangerous conditions and can estimate unbiased naturalistic rates only when likelihood ratios are known and the sampling proposal covers the failure region [f6846, f7262]. Trustworthy rates remain constrained by poorly known naturalistic distributions, high model dependence and potentially huge weight variance; the methods cannot establish high-dimensional robustness or account for unmodelled physics [f7264, f7265, f7266, f7263]. The Michigan precedent reduced simulated exposure but was research rather than a production timeline, did not eliminate model validation or sensor tests, and demonstrated academic—not regulatory acceptance of a production AEB system [f1783, f1784, f1785].
